routes.description: Establish that universally binding moral truths require a nonhuman objective standard, identify that standard with God's immutable and revealed character, and show that secular welfare, preference, convention, and contract accounts cannot supply equivalent moral objectivity or obligation.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if objective moral absolutes are established, God's necessary character is shown to ground both their truth and authority, and the proposed secular standards are shown unable to explain their universality, nonarbitrariness, or prescriptive force.

motionBridge.description: Show that objective moral truth and obligation require God's character as their necessary, nonhuman foundation.

centralBridges.description: Establish that at least some actions possess universally true moral status independent of individual or collective preference.
Explain how God's immutable character, rather than an arbitrary divine choice, constitutes the objective moral standard.
Show why consequence, preference, convention, and contractual agreement cannot generate universally binding moral duties.
Connect God's nature, creative authority, and purposes to prescriptions that bind human agents.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how revelation and divine omniscience provide access to moral requirements and informed guidance about their application.
Use difficult cases to test whether harm-oriented secular standards preserve the moral judgments they purport to explain.

routes.description: Reject the claimed necessity of a divine foundation by distinguishing definitions from objectively assessable judgments, grounding moral inquiry in real consequences, intentions, and impartial rule construction, and showing that divine-nature claims do not independently explain goodness or obligation.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if a coherent secular method can yield objective assessments or justified rules without God, or if the divine account fails to establish moral absolutes, nonarbitrary goodness, or a valid transition from facts about God to binding duties.

motionBridge.description: Show that God is not required for defensible moral truth or obligation because secular inquiry is viable or divine grounding is explanatorily incomplete.

centralBridges.description: Distinguish the selection of a moral standard from the objective truth of judgments concerning suffering, consequences, intentions, and circumstances.
Explain how welfare-sensitive reasoning and impartial contractual construction can justify rules without presupposing divine existence.
Test whether identifying goodness with God's nature makes the divine standard circular, arbitrary, or modally unexplained.
Require an account of how descriptions of God's nature, power, creation, or judgment entail reasons or duties to obey.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish God's possible role as an omniscient source of information from the facts that make conduct morally right or wrong.
Separate the existence or justification of moral requirements from motivation, compliance, punishment, and practical deterrence.

sections.title: Moral Objectivity and the Existence of Absolutes
sections.rationale: Defines the phenomenon requiring explanation and tests whether morality involves intrinsic universal truths, objectively assessable claims under a chosen standard, or context-sensitive judgments about consequences and intentions.

sections.title: Divine Nature, Necessity, and Nonarbitrariness
sections.rationale: Addresses whether God's immutable character supplies a necessary moral standard or leaves unresolved circularity, contrary-nature possibilities, and the basis for calling the divine character good.

sections.title: Secular Welfare and Impartial Rule Construction
sections.rationale: Examines whether facts about suffering, potential conscious states, social consequences, and veil-of-ignorance reasoning can support objective assessments or justified rules without God.

sections.title: Moral Obligation and the Is-Ought Bridge
sections.rationale: Tests how either foundation produces binding prescriptions, with particular attention to whether creation, ownership, divine purposes, definitions, or secular commitments provide reasons agents ought to act.

sections.title: Omniscience, Revelation, and Moral Knowledge
sections.rationale: Distinguishes the metaphysical ground of morality from access to relevant facts and evaluates whether omniscience and revelation establish foundation, reliable guidance, or only informational authority.

sections.title: Counterexamples, Motivation, and Practical Force
sections.rationale: Organizes the disputed cases involving hidden harm, rule consequences, disobedience, punishment, and deterrence to test each account without conflating moral truth with motivation or compliance.

moves.speaker: Matt Slick
moves.proposition: Moral truth requires a mind-grounded, nonarbitrary source, while an atheistic appeal to consequences cannot impose universally binding moral values.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted opening argument is delivered by Matt after Scott explicitly asks him to present his case from the ground up.

response.rationale: This constructive move states the principal necessity argument connecting universal moral truth to a nonhuman mind-grounded source and challenging consequence-based atheistic accounts.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It clearly establishes the opening dispute, though the necessity inference and exclusion of secular alternatives remain compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposition is recoverable, but mind-grounded, nonarbitrary, and universally binding are not sufficiently distinguished or qualified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The excerpt raises a genuine explanatory demand but asserts necessity without excluding non-theistic realist or constructivist alternatives.

charity.alternative: Secular moral realism or impartial constructivism could ground universal judgments without a divine mind.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move must exclude those accounts rather than only consequence assignment.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conclusion depends on an unsupported bridge from universal truth to a mind and then to a divine source.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move relies chiefly on asserted conceptual necessity and supplies no developed comparison with serious secular rivals.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the motion-level claim that objective morality requires a necessary divine or mind-grounded standard.

representationalCharity.rationale: The argument treats atheistic consequence assignment as broadly representative and does not engage stronger secular grounding alternatives.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks how a consequence-based statement acquires universal truth value and denies adequate justification within atheism.

moves.speaker: Scott Clifton
moves.proposition: Secular moral inquiry can adopt the substantive aim of promoting flourishing and reducing unnecessary suffering while recognizing that the definition of morality is not itself a truth claim.
moves.attributionBasis: Scott takes the floor after Matt yields and explicitly contrasts top-down and bottom-up approaches while explaining his own practical moral concern.

components.text: Whether secular morality can specify a substantive evaluative aim rather than inherit a divine standard.
Whether selecting welfare supplies universally binding truth or obligation rather than merely a chosen definition.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the demand for a secular subject matter by naming flourishing and suffering, but it does not yet explain universal authority or truth acquisition.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a partial answer contacting the decisive secular-standard component while leaving universality and binding force unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly separates arbitrary word definitions from the substantive welfare phenomena that the speaker proposes to investigate.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The modest claim that inquiry can adopt this substantive aim is supported by the explicit definitional distinction.

charity.alternative: The opening objection concerns objective authority, not whether humans may choose a topic called morality.
charity.decisiveQualification: A chosen aim does not alone establish universally binding obligation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The definition-versus-substantive-inquiry distinction is coherent, with one remaining bridge from chosen concern to normativity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual distinction is well illustrated, but the welfare standard's authority and completeness are not independently defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central secular-objectivity bridge by distinguishing definitional choice from substantive moral inquiry.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly redirects attention to substantive welfare, although it leaves the strongest authority challenge explicitly unanswered.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly calls words arbitrarily definable while identifying flourishing, well-being, and unnecessary suffering as the substantive concern.

moves.speaker: Matt Slick
moves.proposition: Morality is grounded in God's immutable nature and essence rather than arbitrary commands, and that enduring standard is disclosed through divine self-revelation.
moves.attributionBasis: Matt expressly rejects the divine-command formulation attributed to him and states the character-based Christian account during the ensuing exchange.

components.text: Whether morality has a nonarbitrary standard beyond a humanly selected welfare definition.
Whether divine self-revelation makes moral requirements epistemically accessible.

response.rationale: The response offers God's nature rather than arbitrary command as the standard and adds revelation, directly presenting the rival foundational account.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It fully contacts the foundational contrast, although merely identifying God as the standard does not establish noncircular goodness.

precisionFindings.rationale: The nature-based account is clear, though the distinction between metaphysical grounding and revelatory access remains only implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The account is stated confidently, but immutability alone does not fully warrant nonarbitrariness or moral goodness.

charity.alternative: A nature-based divine theory avoids arbitrary commands but may still face the Euthyphro-style evaluation question.
charity.decisiveQualification: Identifying the standard does not independently explain why that nature is good.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The nature account is internally usable, but the bridge from immutable identity to objective goodness remains materially underdeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The key claims about divine nature and revelation are asserted rather than supported or compared with the secular proposal.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It squarely supports the indispensable central bridge explaining morality through God's immutable character.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move supplies a genuine third formulation but too quickly treats that formulation as disposing of the underlying evaluative challenge.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt distinguishes divine command theory from God's nature and essence, then identifies God as the moral standard.

moves.speaker: Scott Clifton
moves.proposition: God's fixed identity does not explain why an eternally contrary divine nature is impossible, leaving the alleged necessity and nonarbitrariness of the divine moral standard unexplained.
moves.attributionBasis: Scott repeatedly advances and refines the possible-world and hypothetical-world challenge, with Matt's short answers serving as the objects of that sustained examination.

components.text: Whether immutability explains why God has this moral nature rather than an eternally contrary nature.
Whether a mind-grounded standard is thereby nonarbitrary and necessary.

response.rationale: The possible-world questioning directly tests the modal and explanatory bridge from fixed divine identity to necessary nonarbitrary moral character.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive inference and identifies the unexplained modal premise rather than merely changing topics.

precisionFindings.rationale: The challenge clearly concerns explanatory and modal possibility, not the factual claim that the actual God has a fixed identity.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The interrogative force appropriately seeks an explanation and does not claim that a contrary divine nature is established as possible.

charity.alternative: Essential identity may make a contrary nature impossible because such a being would not be God.
charity.decisiveQualification: That semantic or identity response still requires an account of moral necessity rather than mere actual identity.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The objection consistently distinguishes actual immutability from an explanation of why the contrary nature is impossible.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conceptual counterfactual effectively tests the stated inference, with a bounded gap concerning theories of essential identity.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central divine-circularity bridge by challenging necessity and nonarbitrariness in the nature account.

representationalCharity.rationale: The questioning accommodates eternal identity while accurately pressing the remaining explanatory and modal issue.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt grants that God may have an eternal nature and asks what explains possession of that nature rather than another.

moves.speaker: Matt Slick
moves.proposition: A hypothetical that reverses God's essential holy and righteous character cannot test divine morality because it replaces the theological subject whose nature grounds the standard.
moves.attributionBasis: Matt directly answers the proposed alternate divine nature, explains why he will not grant it, and concludes by restating his revealed-character account.

components.text: Whether an imagined being with contrary essential traits would still be the God whose nature grounds morality.
Whether God's revealed actual character supplies a moral standard.

response.rationale: The reply directly rejects the identity assumption in the counterfactual and restates the actual revealed-character account, but does not fully answer the modal challenge.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive hypothetical but only partially answers why the actual divine nature has necessary moral authority.

precisionFindings.rationale: The identity objection is recoverable, but calling the scenario idolatrous blurs theological rejection with logical or modal impossibility.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Replacing the subject may defeat one formulation, but it does not establish that the contrary moral ground is metaphysically impossible.

charity.alternative: The hypothetical tests whether any necessarily existing creator's character would define goodness, not whether that being is the actual God.
charity.decisiveQualification: Renaming the contrary being does not resolve the grounding theory's apparent arbitrariness.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The identity-based response is coherent as far as it goes, but does not entail the claimed defeat of the counterfactual test.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The asserted revealed traits support the actual-account description but not the stronger modal or nonarbitrariness conclusion.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly defends the central divine-nature bridge against the contrary-nature challenge, though incompletely.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response notices an identity issue but substantially narrows the opponent's modal test and omits its decisive theoretical purpose.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt labels the scenario idolatrous, distinguishes redefining God's character, and restates holiness, righteousness, and revelation.

moves.speaker: Scott Clifton
moves.proposition: If God is the sole standard by which God is evaluated, believers lack a noncircular basis for determining that the divine standard is good rather than profoundly harmful.
moves.attributionBasis: Scott clarifies the counterfactual, tests dishonesty for logical impossibility, and then explicitly states the circular-standard objection as the conclusion of his questioning.

components.text: Whether God's nature can be evaluated as good without using that same nature as the sole standard.
Whether rejecting contrary divine character resolves the circular evaluation problem.
Whether a mind-grounded source is thereby nonarbitrary.

response.rationale: The move explicitly identifies self-evaluation as circular and explains the consequence: believers cannot distinguish a good divine standard from a harmful one.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts the decisive inference and states the alleged defeating consequence for nonarbitrary divine grounding.

precisionFindings.rationale: The circularity objection, its target, and its epistemic consequence are all expressly and consistently stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Given the stipulated sole standard, the claimed lack of independent evaluation follows with appropriately strong but not absolute force.

charity.alternative: A foundational standard may be self-authenticating without vicious circularity, as every ultimate standard ends explanation somewhere.
charity.decisiveQualification: The account must still explain why this stopping point warrants moral rather than merely definitional authority.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from sole self-standardization to lack of independent evaluation is strong, with a bounded foundationalist qualification.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The argument is supported by the opponent's stated standard, though rival accounts of ultimate explanation receive limited comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly advances the central divine-circularity bridge against the nature-based account.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection fairly targets epistemic and explanatory circularity, though it does not fully distinguish benign foundational circularity.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that God's nature grounds morality and argues there is no standard for evaluating God other than God himself.

moves.speaker: Scott Clifton
moves.proposition: A divine-nature account supplies no rational reason to obey God when its justification that God is good reduces to the circular claim that God conforms to God's own nature.
moves.attributionBasis: Scott supplies the extended practical example and carries it through the successive questions about wrongness, divine nature, goodness, and reasons for compliance.

components.text: Whether conformity to God's own nature supplies a noncircular rational reason for human obedience.
Whether actual divine identity answers the practical reason-for-obedience problem.

response.rationale: The practical example directly extends the self-certification objection into the normative question of why an agent should conform to divine desires.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the reason-giving demand and states the practical consequence of the alleged circularity.

precisionFindings.rationale: The rational-reason claim is clear, though it implicitly shifts between justification, motivation, and rejection of divine authority.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Circularity weakens the offered justification, but the claim that this alone rationally requires rejection goes beyond the established premise.

charity.alternative: An agent may have reasons grounded in created nature, flourishing, gratitude, authority, or divine purposes beyond the bare goodness definition.
charity.decisiveQualification: Those additional reasons were not supplied in the targeted nature-based justification.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The circular-justification critique is coherent, but its stronger conclusion about rational rejection and motivation is not fully entailed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The practical illustration supports the central concern, while excluding other possible reasons remains insufficiently warranted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central is-ought bridge by demanding a reason why divine nature binds agents.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection fairly exposes the stated circular reason but overstates rejection by not preserving possible independent theistic reasons.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says conformity to God's nature leaves the agent without a rational assessment establishing God as a good moral foundation.

moves.speaker: Matt Slick
moves.proposition: God knows all actual and potential facts, so divine moral revelations may rest on relevant reasons that limited human agents cannot fully understand.
moves.attributionBasis: Matt responds immediately to Scott's practical objection and explicitly invokes divine omniscience to distinguish God from an ordinary human adviser.

components.text: Whether divine guidance may rest on reasons unavailable to epistemically limited human agents.
Whether omniscience independently establishes that God's underlying reasons are morally good.

response.rationale: The response supplies an epistemic reason to defer to an omniscient revealer but does not resolve the circular normative evaluation of that revealer.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is a partial answer contacting informational reliability while leaving the decisive goodness and authority component unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly limits its claim to possible reasons that finite agents may not understand, distinguishing God from an ordinary adviser.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The phrase may not understand properly qualifies the limited epistemic inference from stipulated omniscience.

charity.alternative: The objection concerns moral authority and goodness, not merely whether God possesses more consequence information.
charity.decisiveQualification: Epistemic superiority does not by itself establish the normative standard.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Stipulated omniscience coherently supports superior information, though the inference to justified moral deference needs a normative bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The warrant follows from the stipulated definition of omniscience but does not independently support divine goodness or revelation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary revelation-and-omniscience bridge by explaining possible reasons behind guidance.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response fairly adds an important epistemic consideration but partially substitutes informational reliability for the authority challenge.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that God knows all actual and potential facts and may reveal desires based on reasons humans do not understand.

moves.speaker: Matt Slick
moves.proposition: Because God knows every end result, divine omniscience permits perfect moral judgments and informed prescriptions about which actions agents should and should not perform.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn directly answers Clifton's question about omniscience and consistently presents Slick's divine-knowledge argument.

components.text: Whether God can provide informed action guidance unavailable to limited human reasoners.
Whether consequence knowledge makes God the moral foundation rather than a superior evaluator.

response.rationale: The move directly establishes the informational advantage of omniscience and perfect application, but not that God constitutes the truth-maker of moral value.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It partially answers the practical-guidance demand while leaving the foundational and normative-authority issue unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The consequence-knowledge claim is clear, with the unstated qualification that perfect factual judgment presupposes an evaluative criterion.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Omniscience warrants complete consequence knowledge, but perfect moral judgment additionally requires a defended moral standard.

charity.alternative: Perfect knowledge of outcomes supplies information but does not determine which outcomes ought to be valued.
charity.decisiveQualification: The evaluative criterion remains distinct from factual omniscience.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The informational inference is strong, but the transition from knowing all results to making perfect moral judgments is incomplete.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The stipulated omniscience supports factual knowledge, while the evaluative conclusion lacks a separately defended warrant.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly develops the subsidiary omniscience bridge through perfect knowledge and action guidance.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move recognizes the opponent's consequence method but compresses the decisive distinction between information and normative grounding.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt argues that knowing all end results permits God to reveal actions and make perfect judgments about them.

moves.speaker: Scott Clifton
moves.proposition: If consequences determine which actions are right, omniscience makes God an informational intermediary who communicates those facts rather than the foundation that makes the actions right.
moves.attributionBasis: Clifton explicitly develops a hypothetical theistic concession and draws the intermediary-versus-standard distinction in his own turn.

components.text: Whether omniscient consequence knowledge makes God the moral standard rather than an informational intermediary.
Whether hidden divine reasons establish metaphysical grounding rather than epistemic access.

response.rationale: The reply expressly diagnoses the inference: if consequences make actions right, omniscience transmits relevant facts but does not constitute their moral ground.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It identifies the precise conflation between epistemic access and metaphysical foundation and states the defeating consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conditional nature of the argument and the distinction between intermediary and standard are both plainly stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Within the expressly assumed consequence-grounded scenario, the intermediary conclusion follows without broader overclaim.

charity.alternative: God could both know consequences and ground value through divine nature.
charity.decisiveQualification: The targeted consequence argument itself establishes only informational superiority, not the additional nature-grounding premise.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conditional distinction between truth-making consequences and an agent who reports them is explicit and inferentially complete.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conclusion is strongly supported by the opponent's consequence-based formulation, with only broader hybrid accounts left open.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly and strongly supports the subsidiary information-foundation distinction.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply preserves the possible nature account while accurately limiting what the omniscience argument independently establishes.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt concedes possible deference to an omniscient being while distinguishing the source of information from what makes conduct right.

moves.speaker: Scott Clifton
moves.proposition: As with conventional measurement standards, a moral definition may be selected by humans while particular judgments assessed against that standard remain objectively true or false.
moves.attributionBasis: Clifton introduces and develops the ruler analogy immediately after Slick's objection to subjective standards.

components.text: Whether objective truth can exist in judgments made against a conventionally selected standard.
Whether accurate application requires a uniquely divine evaluator.

response.rationale: The ruler analogy directly answers the claim that human selection makes every resulting judgment subjective by separating standard choice from application truth.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the objectivity inference, although it does not establish that the selected moral standard is normatively authoritative.

precisionFindings.rationale: The analogy carefully distinguishes arbitrary selection of a unit from objective truth or falsity under that unit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The limited claim about conditional objectivity is warranted, without asserting that the standard itself is objectively mandatory.

charity.alternative: Moral objectivity may require objective reasons for selecting the standard, unlike conventional measurement.
charity.decisiveQualification: The analogy establishes objective application but not categorical normativity.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The selected-standard distinction is valid, with one important bridge missing from conditional truth to moral obligation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The measurement analogy specifically supports objective application, though its relevance to categorical morality is bounded.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central secular-objectivity bridge through a clear conditional-objectivity model.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply accurately answers one objectivity claim while leaving the strongest moral-authority distinction available.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt uses a conventional foot standard to distinguish arbitrary standard selection from objectively true or false measurements.

moves.speaker: Matt Slick
moves.proposition: Given moral absolutes that require an objective standard, the failure of atheistic systems to justify such a standard leaves the theistic account validated by impossibility to the contrary.
moves.attributionBasis: Slick identifies his eliminative argumentative form and explicitly contrasts atheistic and theistic justification of moral absolutes.

components.text: Whether a chosen secular standard can account for moral absolutes rather than merely conditional measurements.
Whether atheistic welfare accounts exhaust the alternatives to divine grounding.
Whether defeating one secular account independently validates divine grounding.

response.rationale: The move challenges secular justification and states an eliminative inference, but it does not establish the asserted two-option exhaustion or fully refute the secular alternatives.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the moral-absolutes dispute but leaves decisive exhaustiveness and refutation components unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The eliminative proposition is clear, but the scope shifts from discussed atheistic systems to all possible alternatives without qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Automatic validation would require an established exhaustive dichotomy and decisive negation, neither of which the excerpt supplies.

charity.alternative: The relevant options include secular realism, constructivism, pluralism, error theory, and multiple theistic grounding accounts.
charity.decisiveQualification: Refuting one atheistic formulation would not automatically validate the proposed Christian account.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The core inference is a false dilemma unless exhaustive alternatives and actual negation of the rival are independently established.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Moral absolutes and atheistic failure are asserted as premises without representative support or serious rival comparison.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Despite its defects, the move directly advances the motion-level claim of necessary theistic validation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The stated two-option structure materially weakens the live alternative space and drives the central inference.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly says negating one of two options validates the other and asserts both moral absolutes and atheistic failure.

moves.speaker: Matt Slick
moves.proposition: Torturing babies to death merely for pleasure is wrong for everyone, and God's revealed prohibition on murder supplies the standard supporting that universal judgment.
moves.attributionBasis: Slick defines moral absolutes, supplies the torture example, and expressly grounds its truth in divine revelation.

components.text: Whether at least one moral judgment is universally true rather than merely conditional on a selected convention.
Whether revelation explains why the torture prohibition is true.

response.rationale: The example directly asserts a universal moral absolute and identifies divine revelation as the speaker's standard for affirming it.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It fully states the counterexample and proposed ground, though it does not show that secular welfare cannot reach the same judgment.

precisionFindings.rationale: The act, purpose, universal scope, and claimed revelatory basis are sufficiently specified for evaluation.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The universal judgment is strongly intuitive, but revelation's unique grounding role is not established by the example.

charity.alternative: Secular welfare, rights, or contractual accounts can also universally condemn pleasure-motivated torture.
charity.decisiveQualification: Shared condemnation does not identify which theory uniquely grounds the judgment.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The judgment coheres with the stated divine standard, but the example does not inferentially establish that standard's necessity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The case strongly supports broad condemnation, while the exclusive revelatory foundation remains asserted rather than demonstrated.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central moral-absolutes bridge with a clearly universal test judgment.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move supplies a fair test case but does not preserve the strongest secular explanations of the same prohibition.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt condemns torture of babies for pleasure for everyone and grounds that conclusion in revealed prohibitions against murder.

moves.speaker: Matt Slick
moves.proposition: A secret assault on an unconscious person remains wrong even when awareness, pregnancy, disease, discovery, and other stipulated harms are absent, challenging a harm-only moral criterion.
moves.attributionBasis: Slick constructs the coma scenario and expressly applies it as a counterexample to Clifton's stated harm criterion.

components.text: Whether a welfare or harm criterion preserves condemnation when stipulated immediate harms and awareness are absent.
Whether the scenario eliminates potential, rights-based, dispositional, and rule-level harms.

response.rationale: The scenario directly tests a narrow immediate-harm criterion, but it does not contact broader secular accounts involving potential states, rights, risk, or rules.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It partially answers the welfare position by contacting immediate harm while leaving stronger versions of the standard untested.

precisionFindings.rationale: The scenario is clear, but harm is treated narrowly without specifying whether rights, risks, social rules, or potential states count.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The case challenges immediate experiential harm but does not defeat every harm-sensitive or welfare-sensitive moral criterion.

charity.alternative: Harm can include violated interests, risks, counterfactual conscious states, rights, and rule-level social consequences.
charity.decisiveQualification: Absence of awareness or discovery does not stipulate away all such harms.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The counterexample works only under an underdefined narrow harm premise, leaving a substantial equivocation in its conclusion.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The stipulated case is specific, but the claim that there is no relevant harm is insufficiently defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary counterexample bridge by testing harm-oriented secular standards.

representationalCharity.rationale: The example is forceful against a narrow formulation but materially weakens the strongest welfare-sensitive alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt stipulates an unconscious victim, no pregnancy, disease, awareness, discovery, or other immediate identified consequence.

moves.speaker: Scott Clifton
moves.proposition: Secular moral reasoning can evaluate actual and potential conscious states together with rule-level social consequences rather than merely maximizing immediate aggregate happiness.
moves.attributionBasis: Clifton refines his definition and uses the organ-harvesting thought experiment to explain broader consequences of adopting a rule.

components.text: Whether secular evaluation should include potential conscious states and rule-level consequences rather than immediate experienced harm alone.
Whether welfare-sensitive rules can preserve strong prohibitions without revelation.
Whether sophisticated secular consequence reasoning remains a viable alternative.

response.rationale: The reply justifies a broader evaluative demand and illustrates it with organ harvesting, preserving the legitimate counterexample issue while rejecting a narrow snapshot test.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly replaces immediate aggregation with actual, potential, and rule-level consequences and explains why that replacement matters.

precisionFindings.rationale: Actual and potential conscious states and rule-level consequences are clearly identified as distinct parts of the proposed method.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The modest claim that secular reasoning can include these considerations is directly illustrated and appropriately bounded.

charity.alternative: The assault case may concern rights or intrinsic wrongness that consequence expansion still does not fully capture.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move establishes a broader secular reply, not a complete reduction of all wrongness to consequences.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The move coherently expands the evaluative domain and uses rule consequences to answer familiar aggregation objections.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The organ-harvesting illustration provides specific support, with one bounded gap in deriving or choosing the ultimate welfare criterion.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly and strongly supports the central impartial-rules bridge through broadened consequence and rule evaluation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response fairly strengthens the secular account while leaving the intrinsic-rights challenge open rather than pretending to settle it.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly invokes actual and potential conscious states and illustrates broader consequences through an organ-harvesting rule.

moves.speaker: Scott Clifton
moves.proposition: Hypothetical rational construction behind a veil of ignorance can generate impartial rules for social conduct without presupposing the existence or authority of God.
moves.attributionBasis: Clifton introduces a named secular approach and fully explains the rational-choice and veil-of-ignorance mechanism across the boundary lookahead.

components.text: Whether a secular procedure can justify impartial rules without presupposing divine authority.
Whether impartial agents would accept rules permitting hidden assaults.
Whether universally protective rules can be justified contractually.

response.rationale: The veil-of-ignorance construction supplies a concrete secular rule-selection mechanism and therefore directly challenges the asserted absence of alternatives.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It fully contacts the secular-viability demand, though the excerpt does not defend every rational-choice assumption or rule outcome.

precisionFindings.rationale: The hypothetical parties, rationality condition, rule-selection task, and ignorance constraint are all clearly recoverable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move claims a viable justificatory procedure rather than certainty about a unique resulting moral code.

charity.alternative: Contractual agreement may yield fairness without establishing stance-independent moral truth or motivating every actual agent.
charity.decisiveQualification: The motion can still be resisted if a defensible secular method suffices, even without full metaphysical realism.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The impartial-choice mechanism is coherent, with a bounded implicit bridge from hypothetical agreement to actual normative authority.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The mechanism is specifically explained, but assumptions about rationality, bargaining, and binding force receive limited defense.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central impartial-rules bridge with a developed secular justificatory procedure.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move accurately presents an impartial construction and does not needlessly claim more metaphysical objectivity than it establishes.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt describes perfectly rational agents negotiating social rules behind a veil that conceals their eventual identities.

moves.speaker: Matt Slick
moves.proposition: A recipient-preference account can assign opposite moral statuses to the same conduct depending on what a recipient wants and therefore cannot furnish an objective standard.
moves.attributionBasis: The alternating dialogue and Slick's explicit second-person criticism clearly attribute this sustained objection to Matt Slick.

components.text: Whether impartial rule construction avoids dependence on any particular recipient's immediate preferences.
Whether the secular account evaluates potential states and rule-level consequences rather than recipient preference alone.
Whether a simple recipient-preference account can assign variable evaluations.

response.rationale: The objection attacks a recipient-preference formulation but does not contact the immediately preceding impartial and rule-consequence accounts that expressly transcend such preferences.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts only a secondary earlier formulation and is a relevant nonanswer to the strongest secular rule account.

precisionFindings.rationale: The variable-preference example is clear, but its conclusion expands from that account to absence of any objective standard.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Opposite preferences do not entail opposite rule-level moral status under the secular account actually presented.

charity.alternative: The secular view evaluates impartial rules, potential states, consent, and consequences rather than treating recipient liking as sufficient.
charity.decisiveQualification: Preference variability is therefore an input to evaluation, not necessarily the whole standard.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The example may refute simple preference subjectivism, but the inference against the stated impartial secular standard is a non sequitur.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The hypothetical supports variability of liking but not the claimed variability of moral status under stronger secular rules.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It centrally supports the secular-insufficiency bridge, though its contact with the strongest opposing account is weak.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response materially reduces the developed secular position to a simple recipient-preference theory.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt argues that recipient liking would make the same assault alternately good or bad and then denies objectivity.

moves.speaker: Scott Clifton
moves.proposition: A divine moral theory can separate right and wrong entirely from suffering, happiness, and health because a divine nature favoring universal misery would make misery moral by definition.
moves.attributionBasis: Clifton introduces the objection as a problem with Slick's worldview and develops the universal-misery hypothetical directly.

components.text: Whether defining goodness by divine nature permits a contrary nature that makes universal misery morally good.
Whether actual immutability independently explains the goodness of the divine nature.
Whether the divine account has an advantage in preserving welfare-sensitive judgments.

response.rationale: The counterexample directly tests the nature theory's independence from welfare and states the consequence if a misery-favoring nature defines morality.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive grounding premise, though it depends on the disputed coherence of the contrary-nature hypothetical.

precisionFindings.rationale: The in-principle conditional and the universal-misery consequence are both expressly and consistently stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The hypothetical exposes a theoretical implication if coherent, but the excerpt treats the opponent's concession somewhat more conclusively than warranted.

charity.alternative: A perfectly good God's essential nature may make a misery-favoring nature conceptually or metaphysically impossible.
charity.decisiveQualification: Defining perfect goodness through that same nature risks reinstating the circularity under examination.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conditional counterexample is coherent and probative, with one bounded dependence on the disputed modal possibility.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The opponent's nature definition supports the test, though the claimed concession and possibility require fuller verification.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the central divine-circularity bridge with a welfare-sensitive counterexample.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection recognizes an essential-nature answer indirectly but fairly presses the unresolved circular definition.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt argues that a divine nature favoring the worst universal misery would make that misery moral under the stated theory.

moves.speaker: Scott Clifton
moves.proposition: Even accepting Christianity's factual and moral claims does not by itself supply a motivating reason that compels an agent to obey the divine prescriptions the agent believes are true.
moves.attributionBasis: Clifton explicitly sets up and repeatedly clarifies a role-playing counterexample in which he accepts every proposition in Slick's worldview.

components.text: Whether belief that a divine prohibition is objectively true necessarily supplies motivation to comply.
Whether accepting divine omniscience itself motivates obedience.
Whether moral truth and practical motivation are distinct issues.

response.rationale: The role-playing scenario expressly grants the Christian truth claims while withholding motivation, isolating compliance from ontology and knowledge.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts and cleanly separates the motivational issue, though compelling motivation is stronger than normative reason.

precisionFindings.rationale: The stipulated belief is clear, but motivating reason sometimes shifts between any reason, sufficient motivation, and compulsion.

calibrationFindings.rationale: A possible believer who remains unmotivated suffices to defeat the claim that belief alone necessarily compels compliance.

charity.alternative: Christianity may supply objective reasons even when a vicious agent is not psychologically motivated by them.
charity.decisiveQualification: Failure of motivation does not entail failure of obligation or justification.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The counterexample defeats necessary motivation, but any inference from nonmotivation to absence of normative reason would equivocate.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The stipulated scenario specifically supports the conceptual separation, though it does not establish a broader motivational psychology.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary motivation-ontology distinction.

representationalCharity.rationale: The scenario effectively separates belief from motivation but insufficiently preserves the distinction between reasons and motivational efficacy.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt repeatedly stipulates belief in Christianity and its moral claims while presenting an agent still prepared to commit abuse.

moves.speaker: Matt Slick
moves.proposition: A Christian may knowingly violate acknowledged moral requirements, but inconsistency between profession and practice does not undermine the existence of objective moral truth.
moves.attributionBasis: Slick introduces the revised scenario, cites his counseling experience, and explicitly distinguishes Christian profession from inconsistent practice.

components.text: Whether failure to comply with acknowledged moral truth undermines the existence of objective moral requirements.
Whether the content of the divine standard is independently good.

response.rationale: The reply expressly diagnoses the inference from inconsistent practice to absence of objective truth and states that noncompliance does not bear on truth.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It precisely defeats an ontology-from-compliance inference, while not answering a distinct challenge about sufficient motivating reasons.

precisionFindings.rationale: Professional belief, practical inconsistency, objective truth, and compliance are clearly distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The limited claim that inconsistency does not disprove objective truth follows directly and is properly bounded.

charity.alternative: The opponent's main point may concern motivation rather than an inference against objective truth.
charity.decisiveQualification: The truth-compliance distinction is correct but does not fully answer why the agent has motivating reason.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between truth and compliance is explicit and the limited rebuttal is inferentially sound.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The counseling example illustrates inconsistency, with only a bounded gap in addressing the opponent's actual motivational emphasis.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the subsidiary motivation-ontology bridge by separating truth from compliance.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response accurately defeats one possible inference but only partially addresses the stronger motivational formulation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts Christian profession and practice and explicitly says inconsistency does not prove or disprove objective morality.

moves.speaker: Matt Slick
moves.proposition: Christianity can bridge the is-ought gap because its account includes prescriptions, whereas an arbitrary atheistic system cannot derive a binding ought from descriptions alone.
moves.attributionBasis: The wording expressly defends the prior prescription, invokes the Christian worldview, and contrasts it with Clifton's atheistic system in Slick's argumentative voice.

components.text: What reason makes a divine prescription binding or motivating for an agent who accepts all Christian descriptions.
Whether merely stating a prescription supplies a noncircular reason for obedience.
Whether secular descriptions alone entail categorical prescriptions.

response.rationale: The reply asserts that Christianity contains prescriptions and attacks secular derivation, but it does not supply the requested bridge explaining why those prescriptions bind.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is relevant contrary material but leaves the decisive reason-giving component uncontacted.

precisionFindings.rationale: Prescription, ought, and bridging the gap are treated as equivalent despite the dispute over whether the prescription is justified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Stating that the worldview contains prescriptions does not demonstrate a valid derivation or binding normative reason.

charity.alternative: The objection asks what justifies the prescription, not whether Christian discourse grammatically contains an ought statement.
charity.decisiveQualification: Repetition of an ought is not an is-ought bridge.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The central inference conflates asserting a prescription with deriving or justifying it, leaving the claimed bridge unsupported.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: No independent premise supporting the Christian ought is supplied, and the atheistic impossibility claim is asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attempts the central normative-authority bridge despite failing to complete the inference.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response materially weakens the demand by treating the existence of prescriptive language as the requested justification.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt emphasizes that Slick said a prescription and claims Christianity can bridge is and ought while atheism cannot.

moves.speaker: Scott Clifton
moves.proposition: Facts that God created humanity, is powerful, defines morality, or can punish people remain descriptions that do not by themselves explain why anyone ought to obey God.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker introduces a list of Slick's divine claims as examples and explicitly applies Clifton's recurring descriptive-versus-prescriptive objection to them.

components.text: Whether divine creation, power, standard-setting, and punishment entail a duty to obey.
Whether objective truth alone supplies an agent-relative reason to comply.
Whether description of divine nature itself yields normative authority.

response.rationale: The reply expressly classifies the proffered divine facts as descriptions, identifies the missing entailment, and states that none explains why obedience is required.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly diagnoses the is-ought gap and states the defeating consequence for the claimed Christian bridge.

precisionFindings.rationale: The relevant divine descriptions and the missing duty conclusion are individually specified and consistently distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The limited claim that those descriptions alone do not entail duty is appropriately supported by the identified missing premise.

charity.alternative: Creation, rightful authority, gratitude, teleology, or constitutive human goods might provide the missing normative premise.
charity.decisiveQualification: Those bridge principles are not contained in the listed descriptions themselves.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The diagnosis clearly identifies the missing normative premise and avoids inferring that no theistic bridge could ever exist.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The argument specifically examines each stated divine fact, with only broader unoffered theistic reasons remaining outside its scope.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly and strongly supports the central is-ought bridge by identifying the missing entailment.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection preserves possible theistic bridge premises while accurately finding them absent from the targeted argument.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt lists creation, power, moral-standard status, and punishment, then says none explains why the agent should obey.

moves.speaker: Matt Slick
moves.proposition: People ought to do what is right because right conduct is consistent with and glorifies God, the supreme object of worship and the proper moral standard.
moves.attributionBasis: The response explicitly reiterates what Slick says he has already told Clifton and invokes God's glory, worship-worthiness, and status as the moral standard.

components.text: What normative consideration is offered as the reason agents ought to act consistently with God.
Why God's being the right standard is not circularly assumed in the reason for obedience.
Whether divine glory necessarily motivates an agent who accepts the factual claims.

response.rationale: The response supplies divine glory and worship-worthiness as proposed reasons, contacting the demand, but it does not justify why those facts generate duty or avoid circularity.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is a partial answer that names a reason while leaving its decisive normative warrant and motivational force undefended.

precisionFindings.rationale: The proposed reason is recoverable, but right, glory, greatest object of worship, and right standard mutually reinforce without definition.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion repeats an ought and cites divine status without establishing the normative principle connecting glory or worship-worthiness to duty.

charity.alternative: If humans have a constitutive purpose directed toward divine glory, consistency with that purpose might supply a normative reason.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move does not establish that purpose or explain why agents ought to fulfill it.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The offered reason is intelligible, but the inference is substantially circular because rightness and proper worship are assumed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Divine supremacy, worship-worthiness, and the duty to glorify are asserted without a defended normative bridge.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attempts the indispensable central normative-authority bridge by offering divine glory as the reason for duty.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response gestures toward a teleological bridge but leaves its strongest potentially justificatory premise unstated.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says people ought to do right because it glorifies God, who is the greatest object of worship and right standard.
